--- title: "What's new for time-to-event data in tidymodels" subtitle: "uRos 2026, Paris" author: "Hannah Frick, Posit" title-slide-attributes: data-background-image: images/tidymodels-background.png data-background-size: cover data-background-opacity: "0.3" data-background-color: "#141227" format: revealjs: slide-number: true show-slide-number: all footer: theme: [default, style.scss] css: styles.css highlight-style: a11y width: 1280 height: 720 knitr: opts_chunk: echo: true collapse: true comment: "#>" fig.align: center --- ## Budget participatif :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} - Every year since 2014, Parisians propose and vote on projects - Greening a schoolyard, a new playground, a sports facility, ... - **How long from the vote until the project opens?** ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ![](images/hopscotch-eric-tompkins-unsplash.jpg){height="540" fig-align="center" fig-alt="Colourful numbered stepping stones of a hopscotch game in a playground"} ::: {style="text-align: center; font-size: 0.5em"} Photo by [Eric Tompkins](https://unsplash.com/@erictompkins) on [Unsplash](https://unsplash.com/photos/multicolored-number-boards-tRIw6cFSs2E) ::: ::: :::: ::: {.notes} - city tracks every project from studies through to opening - who would have reached for survival analysis to answer this question? ::: ## The data ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} glimpse(projects) #> Rows: 1,375 #> Columns: 11 #> $ project "3788", "2960", "3594", "12374", "3801", "100… #> $ months 109.23333, 26.00000, 103.00000, 13.23333, 36.… #> $ opened FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, … #> $ theme "social", "sport", "safety", "cleanliness", "… #> $ department "economy", "youth and sports", "roads", "clea… #> $ scale "city-wide", "arrondissement", "arrondissemen… #> $ arrondissement "several", "01", "01", "several", "several", … #> $ priority_share 0.1264368, 0.0000000, 0.0000000, 0.0000000, 1… #> $ edition 2017, 2016, 2017, 2025, 2017, 2021, 2018, 202… #> $ budget 3500000, 200000, 155000, 120000, 3500000, 200… #> $ n_operations 87, 1, 1, 3, 21, 8, 8, 1, 11, 24, 28, 39, 229… ``` ::: [Source: Ville de Paris, opendata.paris.fr, licence ODbL]{style="font-size: 0.6em"} ::: {.notes} - one row per project, editions 2014–2025 (no 2020 edition) - a project counts as open once all of its operations (sites) are open - months: from the vote until opening, or until today if it's not open yet ::: ## Not open yet = censored ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-revealjs/swimmer-short-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Timeline of 12 example projects, each drawn as a horizontal line from its vote, between 2017 and 2025, to its end. Six projects end in a filled dot where they opened. The other six run up to a dashed line marking today and end in an open circle: they are not open yet.' width=1056} ::: ::: Almost 40% of the projects are not open yet ::: {.notes} - we know it's taken *at least* this long, not how long it will take - you all know the drill: pretending they opened today or dropping them both bias the estimates - so: survival analysis ::: ## Time to event ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-revealjs/swimmer-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Timeline of 12 example projects, each drawn as a horizontal line from its vote, between 2017 and 2025, to its end. Six projects end in a filled dot where they opened. The other six run up to a dashed line marking today and end in an open circle: they are not open yet.' width=1056} ::: ::: ::: {.notes} - we know it's taken *at least* this long, not how long it will take ::: ## Everything is an event? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-revealjs/swimmer-all-events-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Timeline of 12 example projects, each drawn as a horizontal line from its vote, between 2017 and 2025, to its end. All twelve end in a filled dot as if they had opened, including the six that are still waiting and whose lines stop at the dashed line marking today.' width=1056} ::: ::: Use the observed time as if every project had opened
→ underestimates the time until opening ::: {.notes} - plain regression on the observed time - the projects still waiting are treated as if they opened today ::: ## Drop the ones still waiting? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-revealjs/swimmer-drop-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Timeline of 12 example projects, each drawn as a horizontal line from its vote, between 2017 and 2025, to its end. The six projects that have opened are shown in full. The six still waiting, which have the longest lines, are faded out.' width=1056} ::: ::: Only use projects that have opened
→ throws away data, and biased: the slow ones are the ones still waiting ::: {.notes} - not missing at random - here: almost 40% are not open yet! - especially recent editions would be left with only their fastest projects ::: ## Survival analysis {visibility="hidden"} - The right tool for _censored regression_ - Despite the name, the event can be loads of things: - A project opening - A business closing - Leaving unemployment or benefits - A household responding during fieldwork ## Kaplan-Meier curve ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-revealjs/km-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Kaplan-Meier curve of the share of projects not yet open over time since the vote, in months. It stays near 100% for the first few months, drops to 50% after roughly 45 months and to about 10% after 130 months. Small tick marks along the curve show censored projects.' width=1056} ::: ::: ::: {.notes} - Time = Months since the vote - Survival prob = prob the project is not yet open - ticks: censored projects, they count as "still waiting" up until they leave the data - later: the null model is exactly this curve, for everyone ::: ## tidymodels ![](images/hex/rsample.png){.absolute top="200" left="0" width="150" fig-alt="rsample hex logo"} ![](images/hex/recipes.png){.absolute top="200" left="250" width="150" fig-alt="recipes hex logo"} ![](images/hex/workflows.png){.absolute top="200" left="400" width="150" fig-alt="workflows hex logo"} ![](images/hex/parsnip.png){.absolute top="200" left="550" width="150" fig-alt="parsnip hex logo"} ![](images/hex/yardstick.png){.absolute top="200" left="800" width="150" fig-alt="yardstick hex logo"} ![](images/hex/tune.png){.absolute top="200" left="1050" width="150" fig-alt="tune hex logo"} ![](images/hex/tidymodels.png){.absolute top="400" left="825" width="250" fig-alt="tidymodels hex logo"} ::: {.notes} - a framework for statistical modelling and machine learning - we take care of the procedural code / boilerplate, so you can focus on the modelling question - consistent interfaces make it easy to explore options: models, preprocessing, metrics, tuning - guardrails against pitfalls such as data leakage make it safe - (click) censored: survival analysis across the whole framework ::: . . . ![](images/hex/censored.png){.absolute top="333" left="626" width="150" fig-alt="censored hex logo"} ## Setting up ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="1-2|4-7|9-12|14-16|18-22"} projects <- projects |> mutate(opening_time = Surv(months, opened), .keep = "unused") set.seed(403) projects_split <- initial_split(projects, prop = 0.8) projects_train <- training(projects_split) projects_folds <- vfold_cv(projects_train, v = 10) projects_rec <- recipe(opening_time ~ ., data = projects_train) |> update_role(project, new_role = "id") |> step_log(budget, n_operations) |> step_other(arrondissement, theme, threshold = 0.02) cox_spec <- proportional_hazards() |> set_engine("survival") |> set_mode("censored regression") projects_metrics <- metric_set( brier_survival, brier_survival_integrated, concordance_survival ) ``` ::: # What's new: models ## Two new engines for random forests ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="|2,6"} ranger_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("ranger") |> set_mode("censored regression") rfsrc_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |> set_engine("randomForestSRC") |> set_mode("censored regression") ``` ::: ::: {.notes} - switching model type or engine is one line - why these? they are fast - why random forests? generally work well out of the box - but also: why tree-based models? censored has quite a few of those! - censored smooths over engine quirks, e.g. randomForestSRC's 0/1 status coding and pre-made Surv responses in recipes ::: ## Survival trees ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-revealjs/tree-illustration-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Survival tree with two splits, each leaf showing a survival curve. Projects from editions 2020 and later form one leaf of 366 projects, whose curve stays above 70% over the five years observed. Earlier editions are split by budget at 64,500 €: for the 189 smaller projects, half are open after about 20 months; for the 545 larger projects, after about 40 months.' width=1152} ::: ::: ::: {.notes} - a forest averages many such trees - each leaf holds a survival curve, not a single number - flexible: no proportional hazards assumption - data-driven groupings ::: ## A null model as your true baseline ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} null_spec <- null_model() |> set_engine("survival") |> set_mode("censored regression") ``` ::: - Ignores all predictors: one Kaplan-Meier curve for everyone - Does your model beat doing nothing? ::: {.notes} - the Kaplan-Meier curve from the start, for every project ::: ## The same prediction for everyone {visibility="hidden"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} null_wflow <- workflow(projects_rec, null_spec) null_fit <- fit(null_wflow, data = projects_train) predict(null_fit, slice(testing(projects_split), 1:3), type = "time") #> # A tibble: 3 × 1 #> .pred_time #> #> 1 46 #> 2 46 #> 3 46 ``` ::: ::: {.notes} - three different projects, same predicted time: the median of the Kaplan-Meier curve ::: ## Predicting survival probabilities {visibility="hidden"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} null_pred <- predict( null_fit, slice(testing(projects_split), 1:3), type = "survival", eval_time = c(12, 24, 36, 48) ) null_pred$.pred[[1]] #> # A tibble: 4 × 2 #> .eval_time .pred_survival #> #> 1 12 0.92 #> 2 24 0.752 #> 3 36 0.586 #> 4 48 0.472 ``` ::: ::: {.notes} - probability of not being open yet, at chosen points in time (here every year) - one tibble per project, nested in .pred: still one row per project - the same for every project with the null model - this is the type of prediction the Brier score works with ::: ## Many models at once ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} projects_res <- workflow_set( preproc = list(rec = projects_rec), models = list( null = null_spec, cox = cox_spec, ranger = ranger_spec, rfsrc = rfsrc_spec ) ) |> workflow_map( "fit_resamples", resamples = projects_folds, metrics = projects_metrics, eval_time = 1:96, seed = 1 ) ``` ::: ::: {.notes} - we take care of the procedural code - you focus on the modelling choices: preprocessing, models, metrics - easier to review ::: ## Beating the baseline ::: {.r-stack} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-revealjs/brier-null-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Brier score of the null model, as a dashed line over months since the vote: zero for the first months, rising to a peak of about 0.25 around month 45, then falling to about 0.16 by month 96.' width=1056} ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-revealjs/brier-over-time-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Brier score over months since the vote for the null model, as a dashed line, and for the Cox model, ranger and randomForestSRC. All models are close during the first year. After that, the three models stay clearly below the null model, peaking around 0.2, with randomForestSRC lowest throughout. Late on, after about 85 months, ranger rises above the null model.' width=1056} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.notes} - Brier score: how close the predicted probability is to what happened, at time t (lower is better) - null model first: low at first, almost no project opens in the first months; peaks when it's hardest to tell who's still waiting - (click) the other models - ranger is weaker in the tail: its small default minimum node size keeps the survival curves high late on ::: ## The final model {visibility="hidden"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} best_id <- rank_results( projects_res, rank_metric = "brier_survival_integrated" ) |> slice_head(n = 1) |> pull(wflow_id) final_fit <- projects_res |> extract_workflow(best_id) |> last_fit(projects_split, metrics = projects_metrics, eval_time = 1:96) ``` ::: ::: {.notes} - OPTIONAL slide - rank by integrated Brier score, take the best workflow - last_fit(): fit on all of the training data, evaluate once on the test data ::: ## Predictions are survival curves {visibility="hidden"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-revealjs/example-curves-1.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Predicted survival curves, the probability of not yet being open over 96 months since the vote, for four projects from the 2018 edition. The living environment project with a budget of 590K € is slowest, with about a 40% chance of still not being open after 8 years. The sport (200K €) and culture (650K €) projects end around 15 to 20%, and the education project (250K €) is fastest, ending below 10%.' width=1056} ::: ::: ::: {.notes} - OPTIONAL slide - one curve per project, from the best model - all from the same edition, so the differences come from theme and budget ::: # Built to be extended ## We extend ![](images/hex/rsample.png){.absolute top="200" left="0" width="150" fig-alt="rsample hex logo"} ![](images/hex/recipes.png){.absolute top="200" left="250" width="150" fig-alt="recipes hex logo"} ![](images/hex/workflows.png){.absolute top="200" left="400" width="150" fig-alt="workflows hex logo"} ![](images/hex/parsnip.png){.absolute top="200" left="550" width="150" fig-alt="parsnip hex logo"} ![](images/hex/yardstick.png){.absolute top="200" left="800" width="150" fig-alt="yardstick hex logo"} ![](images/hex/tune.png){.absolute top="200" left="1050" width="150" fig-alt="tune hex logo"} . . . ![](images/hex/spatialsample.png){.absolute top="333" left="76" width="150" fig-alt="spatialsample hex logo"} ![](images/hex/textrecipes.png){.absolute top="333" left="326" width="150" fig-alt="textrecipes hex logo"} ![](images/hex/embed.png){.absolute top="466" left="250" width="150" fig-alt="embed hex logo"} ![](images/hex/workflowsets.png){.absolute top="333" left="476" width="150" fig-alt="workflowsets hex logo"} ![](images/hex/censored.png){.absolute top="333" left="626" width="150" fig-alt="censored hex logo"} ![](images/hex/finetune.png){.absolute top="333" left="1126" width="150" fig-alt="finetune hex logo"} ::: {.notes} - tidymodels is built to be extended - we have extended the core packages ourselves: spatialsample, recipes extensions, parsnip extensions, workflowsets, finetune - not much for yardstick so far ::: ## You extend :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="33%"} [![](images/tidymodels-learn-developer-tools.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="The Learn page on tidymodels.org with the developer tools category highlighted, listing articles such as creating your own broom tidier methods, recipe step function, and score class object."}](https://www.tidymodels.org/learn/#category=developer%20tools) ::: {style="text-align: center"} [Developer articles](https://www.tidymodels.org/learn/#category=developer%20tools) ::: ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} [![](images/parsnip-dev-checklists.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="The Dev checklists article in the Articles menu of the parsnip website, with checklists for adding a new model, adding a new engine, and documenting a new engine."}](https://parsnip.tidymodels.org/articles/checklists.html) ::: {style="text-align: center"} [Checklists](https://parsnip.tidymodels.org/articles/checklists.html) ::: ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} [![](images/tidymodels-skills.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Homepage of tidymodels skills: Claude Code Skills for Tidymodels, to build models or create extensions following best practices."}](https://skills.tidymodels.org) ::: {style="text-align: center"} [Skills](https://skills.tidymodels.org) ::: ::: :::: ::: {.notes} - you can build your own: models, engines, recipe steps, metrics, tidiers - we've written down how: developer articles on tidymodels.org (Learn, developer tools) - the checklists we use ourselves, for new models and engines (parsnip) and for new steps (recipes) - Claude Code skills for tidymodels: for using it, and for creating extensions following our practices ::: ## You extend: developer articles [![](images/tidymodels-learn-developer-tools.png){height="500" fig-align="center" fig-alt="The Learn page on tidymodels.org with the developer tools category highlighted, listing articles such as creating your own broom tidier methods, recipe step function, and score class object."}](https://www.tidymodels.org/learn/#category=developer%20tools) []{style="font-size: 0.6em"} ::: {.notes} - you can build your own: models, engines, recipe steps, metrics, tidiers - we've written down how: tidymodels.org, Learn, developer tools ::: ## You extend: checklists [![](images/parsnip-dev-checklists.png){height="500" fig-align="center" fig-alt="The Dev checklists article in the Articles menu of the parsnip website, with checklists for adding a new model, adding a new engine, and documenting a new engine."}](https://parsnip.tidymodels.org/articles/checklists.html) []{style="font-size: 0.6em"} ::: {.notes} - the checklists we use ourselves, for new models and engines - in the Articles menu of the parsnip website - recipes has one for new steps: ::: ## You extend: skills [![](images/tidymodels-skills.png){height="500" fig-align="center" fig-alt="Homepage of tidymodels skills: Claude Code Skills for Tidymodels, to build models or create extensions following best practices."}](https://skills.tidymodels.org) []{style="font-size: 0.6em"} ::: {.notes} - Claude Code skills for tidymodels: for using it, and for creating extensions following our practices ::: ## Something missing? Ask us! [![](images/issue-551.png){width="820" fig-align="center" fig-alt="Closed GitHub issue 551 in yardstick, titled New survival metric type for linear_pred predictions. The user asks for a metric type that triggers linear predictor predictions, so they can write metrics such as Royston and Sauerbrei's R²_D."}](https://github.com/tidymodels/yardstick/issues/551) . . . → yardstick: a new metric type for the linear predictor, and `royston_survival()` ::: {.notes} - a user wanted to write their own metrics on the linear predictor - that wasn't possible: no metric type triggered that kind of prediction - they asked, we built it - they also wanted Royston and Sauerbrei's metric, so we added that as well - the same user also asked for easier access to censoring weights in predict() (parsnip #1371) ::: ## Royston's metric {visibility="hidden"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} workflow(projects_rec, cox_spec) |> fit_resamples( projects_folds, metrics = metric_set(royston_survival, concordance_survival) ) |> collect_metrics() #> # A tibble: 2 × 6 #> .metric .estimator mean n std_err .config #> #> 1 concordance_survival standard 0.736 10 0.0107 pre0_mod0_post0 #> 2 royston_survival standard 0.355 10 0.0205 pre0_mod0_post0 ``` ::: ::: {.notes} - how well the linear predictor separates the projects - mixes with existing metric types in the same metric set - needs a linear predictor: Cox, Weibull, boosted tree, but not the forests or the null model - royston_survival() reports R²_D, the explained-variation version of D ::: ## What's new - Random forests via `"ranger"` and `"randomForestSRC"` - A null model as a baseline - A new metric type for the linear predictor, and Royston-Sauerbrei's metric - Also new: faster tuning for boosted trees, censoring weights in `predict()`
::: {style="text-align: center"} ::: ::: {.notes} - boosted trees with mboost: multi_predict(), so tune_grid() fits one model per number of trees ::: ## Durations with unfinished cases? - Project openings, business closures, unemployment spells, fieldwork response, ... - Censored regression in tidymodels works just like classification or regression - If something is missing, you can extend the framework, or ask us
::: {style="text-align: center"} ::: # Backup {visibility="uncounted"} ## Case weights {visibility="uncounted"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} |model |with case weights |without | |:----------------------|:----------------------------------------|:-------| |proportional_hazards() |survival, glmnet | | |survival_reg() |survival, flexsurv, flexsurvspline | | |decision_tree() |rpart, partykit | | |bag_tree() | |rpart | |boost_tree() | |mboost | |rand_forest() |partykit, aorsf, ranger, randomForestSRC | | ::: ::: ::: {.notes} - censored 0.4.0: bag_tree() with rpart and boost_tree() with mboost no longer accept case weights - ipred errors with weights; mboost fits with weights but can't predict from those fits ::: ## Coming from SAS {visibility="uncounted"} | SAS | R/tidymodels | |---|---| | `PROC LIFETEST` | `survival::survfit()`, `null_model()` | | `PROC PHREG` | `proportional_hazards()` | | `PROC LIFEREG` | `survival_reg()` | ::: {.notes} - same models, different defaults: PHREG uses Breslow for ties (R: Efron), LIFETEST uses log-log CIs (R: log) ::: ## Data caveats {visibility="uncounted"} - Opening dates are given to the month - The vote is approximated as 1 October of the edition year - Source: Ville de Paris, *Budget participatif : opérations des projets gagnants et réalisations*, opendata.paris.fr, licence ODbL ## Abandoned projects {visibility="uncounted"} - About 5% of operations are abandoned: they will never open - That's a competing risk; here we dropped them

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
